source_text: Sed illo genere magis urgendi sunt, ut intellegant, si possunt, quam uere in catholica dicatur omnium naturarum esse auctorem deum. quo de genere superius agebam, cum dicerem: uitupero tecum pestem, caecitatem, caenositatem turbidam, horribilem uehementiam, corruptibilitatem, inmanitatem principum et his similia; lauda tu mecum speciem, distinctionem, ordinationem, pacem, unitatem formarum, mem- \'brorum congruentias et numerosas parilitates, uitalia spiramenta et nutrimenta, temperamentum salutis, regimen et moderamen animae famulatusque corporum, similitudinem concordiamque partium in singulis naturis uel quae habitabant uel quae habitabantur et cetera huiusmodi. sic enim intellegunt, si tamen sine pertinacia uelint adtendere, iam et bona et mala se miscere, cum loquuntur de illa terra, ubi solum et summum malum fuisse crediderunt, itaque, si tollantur illa, quae mala enumerata sunt, bona illa, quae laudata sunt, sine ulla uituperatione remanere; si autem bona ipsa tollantur, nullam remanere naturam. ex quo iam uidet, qui potest uidere, omnem naturam, in quantum natura est, bonum esse, quia ex una eademque re, in qua et ego, quod laudarem, et ille, quod uituperaret, inuenit, si tollantur ea, quae bona sunt, natura nulla erit; si autem tollantur ea, quae displicent, incorrupta natura remanebit. tolle de aquis, ut sint caenosae et turbidae, remanent aquae purae atque tranquillae; tolle de aquis partium concordiam, non erunt aquae. si ergo malo illo adempto manet natura purgatior, bono autem detracto non manet ulla natura, hoc ibi facit naturam, quod bonum habet; quod autem malum, non natura, sed contra naturam est. tolle de uentis horrorem et nimium inpetum, qui tibi displicet, potes cogitare uentos lenes atque moderatos; tolle de uentis partium similitudinem, qua eorum corpus in unitatem continuatur et sibi pacatur, ut corpus sit, nulla suberit natura, quam cogites. longum est persequi cetera; sed manifestum est eis, qui nullo studio partium iudicant, cum istae naturae commemorantur, adiungi eis quaedam, quibus displiceant; quae cum detrahimus, naturae meliores manent. unde intellegitur eas, in quantum naturae sunt, bonas esse, quia cum eis uicissim omne, quod bonum habent, detraxeris. naturae nullae erunt. animaduertite etiam, qui recte uultis iudicare, illum quoque principem inmanem; cui si auferatur inmanitas, adtendite quanta laudabilia remanebunt: conpago corporis, membrorum hinc atque inde. congruentia, formae unitas et pax contextarum inter se partium, animae regentis et uegetantis famulantisque et uegetati corporis ordo et dispositio. quae omnia si auferantur, et si qua forte minus enumeraui, nulla prorsus natura subsistet.
thought_title: Goods and evils in the land of darkness
orientation: Augustine is arguing that the Manichaean land of darkness cannot be pure evil, because it contains goods that remain when its evils are removed.
pass_a_gloss: But they must be pressed rather by that kind of argument, so that they understand, if they can, how truly it is said in the Catholic Church that God is the author of all natures. About which kind I was dealing above, when I said: I blame with you the plague, blindness, turbid filthiness, horrible violence, corruptibility, the savagery of the rulers, and things similar to these; you praise with me the form, distinction, ordering, peace, unity of forms, the congruences of members and numerous equalities, the vital breathings and nourishments, the tempering of health, the rule and guidance of the soul and the service of bodies, the likeness and concord of parts in each nature, both those which inhabited and those which were inhabited, and other things of this kind. For thus they understand, if only they are willing to attend without obstinacy, that they are already mixing goods and evils, when they speak about that land where they believed there was only and supreme evil, and so, if those things which have been enumerated as evils are removed, those goods which have been praised remain without any blame; but if the goods themselves are removed, no nature remains. From this he already sees, who can see, that every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good, because from one and the same thing, in which both I found what I would praise and he found what he would blame, if those things which are good are removed, there will be no nature; but if those things which displease are removed, an incorrupt nature will remain. Take from waters that they be filthy and turbid, pure and tranquil waters remain; take from waters the concord of parts, they will not be waters. If therefore, when that evil is removed, a purer nature remains, but when the good is taken away, no nature remains, what makes nature there is what good it has; but what is evil is not nature, but against nature. Take from winds the horror and excessive force which displeases you, you can think of winds gentle and moderate; take from winds the likeness of parts, by which their body is continued into unity and is at peace with itself, so that it is a body, no nature will remain for you to think of. It is long to pursue the rest; but it is manifest to those who judge with no zeal for parties, when these natures are mentioned, that certain things are joined to them by which they displease; when we take these away, better natures remain. From this it is understood that they, insofar as they are natures, are good, because when you have in turn taken away from them everything good that they have, there will be no natures. Notice also, you who wish to judge rightly, that savage ruler himself; if savagery is taken away from him, attend how many praiseworthy things will remain: the compactness of the body, the congruence of members on this side and that, the unity of form and the peace of parts woven together among themselves, the order and arrangement of the soul ruling and giving life and of the body serving and being given life. If all these things are taken away, and if perhaps I have enumerated too few, no nature at all will subsist.

choices.why: Keeps the two nouns as distinct qualities, matching the source's paired terms for the foulness of the land of darkness.
Renders inmanitas as savagery to convey the violent, monstrous quality Augustine attributes to Mani's rulers of darkness.
Preserves the plural abstract nouns and the adjective uitalia as vital, matching the source's list of goods in created natures.
Temperamentum means a proper mixture or balance; rendering as tempering keeps the sense of a balanced condition that constitutes health.

choices.english: the rule and guidance of the soul
choices.why: Both regimen and moderamen denote governing; using two distinct English nouns preserves the source's double expression.
rejected: the rule and control of the soul
the governance and guidance of the soul

choices.why: Famulatus is the state of being a servant; service captures the body's subordinate role to the soul.

pass_b_english: But they must be pressed more by that line of argument, so that they may understand, if they can, how truly it is said in the Catholic Church that God is the author of all natures. I was dealing with this line of argument above, when I said: I join you in blaming the plague, the blindness, the turbid filthiness, the horrible violence, the corruptibility, the savagery of the rulers, and things like these. But you join me in praising form, distinction, ordering, peace, the unity of forms, the congruence of members and their equalities in number, the vital breathings and nourishments, the tempering of health, the rule and guidance of the soul and the service of bodies, the likeness and harmony of parts in each nature—both those that inhabited and those that were inhabited—and other things of this kind. For in this way they understand, if they are willing to pay attention without stubbornness, that they themselves are already mixing goods and evils when they speak about that land where they believed there was only supreme evil, and so that if the things that were listed as evils are taken away, the goods that were praised remain without any blame, but that if the goods themselves are taken away, no nature remains. From this, whoever can see now sees that every nature, insofar as it is a nature, is good. For from one and the same thing, in which I found what to praise and he found what to blame, if the things that are good are taken away, there will be no nature; but if the things that displease are taken away, an incorrupt nature will remain. Take from waters that they be filthy and turbid, and pure and tranquil waters remain. Take from waters the harmony of their parts, and they will not be waters. If, therefore, when that evil is removed a purer nature remains, but when the good is taken away no nature remains, then what makes a nature there is the good it has; and what is evil is not a nature, but against nature. Take from winds the dread and excessive force that displeases you, and you can think of winds that are gentle and moderate. Take from winds the likeness of their parts, by which their body is joined into unity and made at peace with itself so that it is a body, and no nature will remain for you to think of. It would take long to go through the rest. But it is clear to those who judge without any partisan zeal that when these natures are mentioned, certain things are attached to them that cause displeasure; and when we remove those things, better natures remain. From this it is understood that they are good insofar as they are natures, because when you take away from them in turn everything good that they have, no natures will exist. Notice also, you who wish to judge rightly, that savage ruler himself. If his savagery is taken away, consider how many praiseworthy things remain: the frame of his body, the congruence of his members on this side and that, the unity and peace of his form with its parts woven together, the order and arrangement of the soul that rules and gives life and of the body that serves and is given life. If all these things are taken away—and any others I may have failed to list—no nature at all will remain.

last_rejected.quote: both those that inhabited and those that were inhabited
last_rejected.source_quote: uel quae habitabant uel quae habitabantur
last_rejected.why: Latin middle/passive 'habitabantur' means 'dwelt in' not 'were inhabited'; contrast is between inhabitants and dwellings.
last_rejected.fix: both those that dwelt and those that were dwelt in
last_rejected.ruling: 'were inhabited' is valid passive of habitare; 'dwelt in' is preference, not error

problems.quote: And so, if the things that were listed as evils are taken away, the goods that were praised remain without any blame. But if the goods themselves are taken away, no nature remains.
problems.source_quote: itaque, si tollantur illa, quae mala enumerata sunt, bona illa, quae laudata sunt, sine ulla uituperatione remanere; si autem bona ipsa tollantur, nullam remanere naturam
problems.why: The infinitives remanere still depend on intellegunt: this is what they understand, not Augustine's own assertion.
problems.fix: and so that if the listed evils are taken away, the praised goods remain without blame, but if the goods themselves are taken away, no nature remains
problems.ruling: 'itaque... remanere; si autem... remanere' are infinitives dependent on 'intellegunt'; English asserts them as Augustine's own claims rather than what the opponents understand.
